sections.title: Word Order
sections.content:
Word Order

Contrary to popular belief, Czech word order is not completely free. In Czech, word order serves to show what you want to stress. The general rule is What you want to stress goes at the end of the sentence. For instance, take the simplest possible sentence Petr pije kolu. (Petr is drinking coke.) The words in this sentence can be ordered in any way and it will still mean the same (unlike English where Coke is drinking Peter is a little awkward). BUT. Each of the orderings serves as an answer to a different question.

Question Answer
Co pije Petr? (What is Petr drinking?) Petr pije kolu.
Kdo pije kolu? (Who is drinking coke?) Kolu pije Petr.

Therefore, unlike English, from even a very simple answer you can guess what the question was. Notice that the answers are mirror images of their questions.

Note: As you may see below the other possible combinations also make sense in Czech

Jí kolu Petr?

Petr kolu pije. (No, Petr doesn't eat coke he drinks it)

Jí Petr kolu?

Kolu Petr pije.

Pije Petr kolu? (not mléko, or čaj)

Pije kolu Petr? (not Jana, or Karel)

(these two combinations would be most likely perceived as questions)

Three words, thus, give us six possible combinations, and all have a slightly different meaning in Czech. The word order is always a little vague for even in English you have sentences like see it he did, Petr he saw, Petr saw he. To grasp the subtle differences you have to live with the language for a long time.

Typical Word Order of a Czech Sentence

Simple sentence

1 2 3 4
subject verb indirect object object
Petr píše Martině dopis.
Petr is writing to Martina a letter.

Note: 3 and 4 are interchangeable.

Sentence with adverbials

1

2

3

4

5

6

adverbial

of time

verb

subject

indirect object

object

adverbial

of place

Včera

psal

Petr

Martině

dopis

v parku.

Yesterday

was writing

Petr

to Martina

a letter

in the park.

!
  • Any part of the sentence could be moved at the end to be stressed:

  • Petr psal Martině dopis v parku VČERA. (not the day before)

  • Dopis psal včera v parku Martině PETR. (not Jirka)

  • Petr psal včera v parku Martině DOPIS. (not a poem)

  • Petr psal včera v parku dopis MARTINĚ. (not to Jana)

  • Petr včera dopis Martině v parku PSAL. (not read)

    Note: The finite verb tends to keep the second position. (if unstressed)

  • The adverbial of time usually precedes that of space.
    Otherwise the position of adverbials is fairly flexible

  • si, se, mě, mi, ti, se, si, ho, mu (jsem, ..., jste in byl jsem,..., byli jste)

  • always take the second position in the sentence

  • Měl jsem se ho zeptat. (I should have asked him.)

  • adjectives always precede nouns - dobrý učitel, malý muž, žlutý banán
    (the reverse - French like - order is possible but would sound archaic)

How does se change around in a sentence?

It in fact se doesn't move at all. se always occupies the second position in the sentence, and other words move around it to allow for that.

1 2 3 4
Jak se jmenuješ?
Jmenuju se Petr.
Jak se máš?
Mám se dobře.
Jak se má Petr?
Petr se má dobře.

Where are jsem and budu placed in the past and future tense?

The auxiallry form of the verb to be (jsem, jsi, jsme, jste) in the past tense is almost always in the second position.

1 2 3 4 5
Koupil jsem si to včera.
Včera jsem si to koupil.
Koupil jsi to včera.
Díval jsem se na televizi.
Tak jsem se Díval na televizi.

The auxiliary form of the verb to be (budu), can be anywhere in the sentence depending on the emphasis on. For example:

  • Zítra budu psát knihu. (Tomorrow, I will be writing a book).

  • Budu zítra psát knihu? (Will I be writing a book tomorrow?)

  • Zítra knihu psát budu. (I will [definitely] be writing a book tomorrow.)

  • Zítra budu knihu psát. (Writing is what I will be doing with the book tomorrow).

Questions and answers in Czech

co? kdo? kdy? kde? kam? proč?

Co píše Petr?

Petr píše dopis.

Kdo píše dopis?

Dopis píše Petr.

Kdy čte Martina?

Martina čte večer.

Kde se učili studenti?

Studenti se učili v parku.

Kam šly děti?

Děti šly do školy.

Proč chcete jíst?

Chceme jíst, protože ... .

!

  • if a question starts with a question word the word order of the answer mirrors

  • the intonation of this kind of question is identical with that of simple statements

ano nebo ne

Píše Petr dopis?

Ano.

Petr píše dopis.

Píše dopis Petr?

Ano.

Dopis píše Petr.

Čte Martina večer?

Ano.

Martina čte večer.

Šly děti do školy?

Ano.

Děti šly do školy.

Učili se studenti v parku?

Ano.

Studenti se učili v parku.

Chcete jíst?

Ano.

Chceme jíst.

!

  • in YES/NO questions you typically swap the verb and the noun

  • however, if your question requires a YES or NO answer, ano or ne will suffice

  • the word order of an answer to a YES/NO question is your typical word order for simple statements

  • the intonation of this type of question has a rising pattern - it goes up on the last syllable in the utterance

Negation

The negative particle ne behaves differently in different tenses. Most of the time it is attached directly to the main verb. Only in the future with budu, budu is negated instead.

Yes No
Past dělal jsem to nedělal jsem to I wasn’t doing it
Present dělám to nedělám to I’m not doing it
Conditional dělal bych to nedělal bych to I wouldn’t do it
Future budu to dělat nebudu to dělat I’m not going to do it.

Note: Sentences like Nejsem to dělal. Nebych jela. or Budu to nedělat. are wrong.

Double Negatives

In Czech, double negatives are a requirement! All pronouns and adverbs used to quantify have to be used in the negative form in addition to the verb in negative form.

ANO NE
Mám všechno. Nemám nic. I have everything / nothing.
Ví všechno. Neví nic. She knows everything / nothing.
Mám nějaký rohlík. Nemám žádný rohlík. I have some bread / no bread.
Příjde vždycky ráno. Nepřijde nikdy. He always comes… / He never comes.

Reference Pronouns (Anaphors)

No language likes to repeat nouns over and over. Instead, pronouns are used to refer back to nouns mentioned before. For example, instead of saying He bought a new car. The car was expensive. you say He bought a new car. It was expensive. You can also refer back to verb or whole sentences. For example, I ran a mile under 10 minutes. It was very difficult.

English uses many pronouns for this purpose: he, she, it, him, her, his

There are several things to remember about Czech in this respect.

  • The pronoun has to match the gender.

  • The pronoun may change according to case, especially after prepositions.

  • The pronoun doesn’t always have to be expressed.

    Nouns unexpressed pronoun Petr má nové kolo.
    Je červené.    		 Petr has a new bike.
    It is read.
    on, ona Jana si koupila knihu, ale
    ona nebyla dobrá.    		 Jana bought a book but
    it wasn’t good.
    mě, jemu, ji, jí Petra nepřinesla tužku,
    protože ji nemohla najít.    		 Petra didn’t bring a pen
    because she couldn’t find it.
    s ním, bez něho Mám dobrý počítač,
    bez něho nemůžu pracovat.    		 I have a good computer,
    without it I cannot work.
    Verbs to Včera jsem ujel 100 km,
    bylo to těžké.    		 Yesterday, I drove 100 km, it was difficult.
    s tím Nemám peníze.
    S tím se nedá nic dělat.    		 I have no money. There’s nothing to be done about it.

Relative Clauses and Phrases

Relative clause or phrase is always begun with a relative particle. See Conjunctions for a list. The important thing to remember about the relative conjunctions (pronouns) který (which), kdo (who), jaký (what) is that they change with the case and gender of the noun they refer to. Co (what) can be used with any case without change.

Který

Který can be translated into English as who, what, that, which. More often than not, English drops the relative pronoun, Czech never does. Který is always preceded by a comma.

Kdo? Co? muž, který přišel,
auto, které nejede		 man who came,
car that doesn’t run
Koho? Co? muž, kterého jsem viděl,
žena, kterou znám
auto, které jsem koupil		 the man I saw
the woman I know
the car I bought
Koho? Čeho? muž, kterého jsem se zeptal
město, do kterého jsem přijel		 the man I asked
city in which I arrived
Komu? Čemu? kamarád, kterému jsem telefonoval
žena, které jsem to řekl		 a friend I called
woman who I told it to
Kom? Čem? muž, o kterém jsme mluvili
země, ve které je svoboda		 man about whom we talked
country in which there is freedom
Kým? Čím? člověk, se kterým se znám
žena, se kterou přišel		 man who I know
woman with who I came

Kdo

Kdo (who) is used differently from English. It is common only in set phrases and only for TEN nouns. Kdo is always preceded by a comma. For other genders, který or co is used.

Kdo? Co? ten, kdo přišel he who came
Koho? Co? ten, koho znám he who I know
Komu? Čemu? ten, komu to dám he who I give it to
Kým? Čím? ten, s kým přijdeš he with whom you come

Co

In colloquial Czech, you can use co (what) in any relative clause regardless of gender or case. The object must also be expressed again by a pronoun in all transitive verbs where in cases other than Kdo? Co?.

Kdo? Co? muž, co přišel,
auto, co nejede		 man who came,
car that doesn’t run
Koho? Co? muž, co jsem ho viděl,
žena, co ji znám		 the man I saw
the woman I know
Koho? Čeho? muž, co jsem se ho zeptal
město, co jsem do něj přijel		 the man I asked
city in which I arrived
Komu? Čemu? kamarád, co jsem mu telefonoval
žena, co jsem jí to řekl		 a friend I called
woman who I told it to
Kom? Čem? muž, co jsme o něm mluvili
země, co v ní je svoboda		 man about who we talked
country in which there is freedom
Kým? Čím? člověk, co se s ním znám
paní, co jsem s ní přišel		 man who I know
woman who I came with

Sentences without Subject

See how these are used as idioms under Idioms, Phraseology and Vocabulary.

Weather - impersonal states

Prší. It's raining. Bude pršet. Pršelo.
Sněží. It's snowing. Bude sněžit. Sněžilo.
Mrzne. It's freezing. Bude mrznout. Mrzlo.
Hřmí. There's thunder. Bude hřmít. Hřmělo.
Blýská se. There's lightning. Bude se blýskat. Blýskalo se.
Taje. There's a thaw. Bude tát. Tálo.

je + adverb

This construction is used most often for describing states of weather, time, etc.

Jak je venku? How's the weather outside? Jak bude venku? Jak bylo venku?
Je teplo. It is warm. Bude teplo. Bylo teplo.
Je horko. It is hot. Bude horko. Bylo horko.
Je hezky. It is nice. Bude hezky. Bylo hezky.
Je chladno. It is cold. Bude chladno. Bylo chladno.
Je zima. It is cold. Bude zima. Byla zima.
Je pět hodin. It's five o'clock. Bude pět hodin. Bylo pět hodin.

Feelings - je + Komu? Čemu? + adverb

Jak je ti? How are you feeling? Jak ti bude? Jak ti bylo?
Je mi dobře. I'm feeling well. Bude mi dobře.Bylo mi dobře.
Je mi zima. I'm cold. Bude mi zima. Bylo mi zima.
Je mi špatně. I'm feeling sick. Bude mi špatně. Bylo mi špatně.
Je mi teplo. I'm hot. Bude mi teplo. Bylo mi teplo.
Je mi smutno. I'm feeling sad. Bude mi smutno. Bylo mi smutno.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.content:
Pronunciation

Pronunciation of individual sounds

Czech prounciation is not particularly difficult. It is about as hard as it is to pronounce any language, if it does not happen to be the one you grew up with. This is because your muscles just find it hard to adjust to new things. It is true, however, that pronunciation is often the most difficult part for adult learners and adults very rarely achieve native-like accent.

It is still important to practice pronunciation when learning Czech because Czech native speakers tend to value correct pronunciation over grammar when interacting with non-native speakers. A student of Czech will have an easier time trying to converse with natives speakers when getting the basics of pronunciation right.

Vowels

There are a few peculiarities in Czech that tend to cause problems for English-speaking mouths. The most troublesome is the pronunciation of vowels.

1) no matter where they are in the word, Czech vowels never loose their full quality, and are always pronounced fully and unflaggingly.

2) each Czech vowel can be either short or long. Long vowels are exactly two times longer than their short brothers. It is very frequent that vowel length changes meaning of words significantly. For instance, děla (cannons) is differentiated from dělá (s/he is working) only by the long á in the latter, and there are even more embarrassing examples. The length of vowels is completely independent on the stress. The stress is always on the first syllable in all Czech words. It is a very frequent that a long vowel occurs in an unstressed position as in dělá. There are two diphthongs ou, au and eu that are pronounced fully, as well.

Consonants

Czech consonants are much less awkward. There are many that are the same as or very similar to those in English. There are five, however, that are not in English at all: ch, ď, ť, ň, ř

  • of the above ř is the most feared one; it is famous for its quirky nature and soft gurgling sound; it is the sound that Czech children learn last (around 5 – 6 years), and a certain portion of the population, including former President Havel, never learn to do it quite right; except for its fame and difficulty (it has been claimed that Czechs invented it deliberately to make Czech harder to learn) ř has little importance for learning the language, and many Czechs will be disappointed if you learn it well, which you very likely will

  • ch is the same as in Scottish loch but mispronouncing it will cause no disasterous misunderstandings;

  • ď, ť, ň, on the other hand have no claims to fame but play a much more important role in the language because they often distinguish between different meanings of similar words

There are even more issues with sounds which are in both English and Czech but are pronounced just a little differently in Czech. For instance, k, p, t don't have aspiration, so it will be difficult for you to distinguish them from g, b, d when they are the first sound in a word. Czech r's are rolled very much like the Scottish r's. Finally, unlike English, Czech h is voiced, which probably makes it the most difficult of Czech sounds for English speakers. Other than that, there's nothing in Czech that will surprise you.

Contrasts

There are several groups of sounds which have something in common one way or another. Vowels and consonants are one example. Vowels are long and short. Consonants are soft and hard, or voiced and unvoiced. It is important to be aware of this opposition since very often when the form of a word changes the ending consonant changes from hard to soft. See the how to spell it charts below for examples.

Short and long vowels

There are many pairs of Czech words which are distinguished only by the length of the vowels.

Soft, hard and neutral consonants

This distinction is important for the choice of i or y which are pronounced identically but spelled depending on the preceding consonant.

hard d t n ch k h g r [-y]
soft ď ť ň š c, č z ž ř j [- i]

The distinction between soft and hard consonants is very important for Czech.

One of the less important implications is the spelling of i and y which are pronounced the same. The i only follows soft consonants, and y hard.

But models of nouns and adjectives are also divided into hard and soft depending on the final consontant. Soft and hard models have different endings.

There is also a group of sounds that are neutral. Neither soft nor hard.

neutral b f l m p s v [- i ]/[-y]

Czechs have to learn by heart which of the neutral consonants are followed by i or y. The default is i with a list of exception that has to be memorised by every Czech school child.

Voiced vs unvoiced (voiceless)

Some consonants are voiced and some are unvoiced (or voiceless). In Czech, it is very important to be aware of the difference because all voiced consonants become unvoiced at the end of words. For instance, muž (man) is pronounced muš. The other rule is that there can only be two consonants of the same quality next to each other, and the second governs the first. For instance, kdy (when) is pronounced gdy, etc.

voiced b v d ď g h z ž dž dz ř
unvoiced p f t ť k ch s š č c ř

The following consonants do not have unvoiced counterparts, and therefore are not influenced by nor do they do anything to other consonants: r, l, m, n, j. So e.g. z in znát (to know) does not change to s as it would for instance in zpátky (back). Nor does s followed by n change to z as in sníst (to eat up) as it would in les dole (forest below) pronounced as lezdole. See section on Assimilation below for much more detail.

Note: The last three contrasts only appear in cases of assimilation. The exception is the the loan word džus which forms a minimal pair with another loan word čus. There are other rare loan words where dž appears unassimilated such as maharádža but which do not form minimal pairs with other words.

Note 2: Ř becomes voiceless when next to another voiceless consonant, e.g. it is pronounced voiceless in tři but voiced in čtyři.

Comparing Czech Sounds to English

Pictorial Guide to Pronouncing Selected Czech Sounds

In the pictures below you will see the position of the tongue, the rounding of the lips and the imprint of the tongue on the palate which shows you the shape of the tongue. Only the sounds that are not in English, or tend to pose difficulties for learners of Czech are displayed.
