Vowels are always a little different in all languages. Notice the rounding of the lips and the position of the tongue and try to compare them to how you pronounce. | The things to look for are: rounding and openness of lips, the mass of the | | tongue low or high, or in the back or in the front. |

Pronouncing syllables, words and sentences

This section describes what happens when we go beyond the pronunciation of individual sounds.

End of word devoicing

All consonants at the end of a word are pronounced unvoiced. This is often only in one or two of their declined or conjugated forms. When a word is spelled with a voiced consonant at the end, there are other forms (for instance including a vowel) where it is pronouced voiced. Here are some common patterns for nouns and verbs.

Devoiced nominative masculine singular

Many masculine nouns (of all models) end in a voiced consonant which is devoiced in the nominative singular and voiced in all other forms where an ending is added.

Masc Sg Masc Pl
hrad hrady
kamarád kamarádi
stav stavy
batoh batohy
dub duby
mráz mrazy
muž muži

Devoiced feminine genitive plural

Many femine nouns of the voda model have a voiced consonant before the final a. They are devoiced in the Plural Genitive.

Fem Sg Fem Gen Pl
voda vod
rada rad
kráva krav
váha vah
doba dob
váza váz

Devoiced impetatives

In some models, the final consonant in the imperative is devoiced.

Verb (3rd Sg) Imperative (Sg)
radí raď
řídí řiď
sedí seď
plave plav
chlubí chlub
leze lez
leží lež

Devoicing homophones

Final consonant devoicing results in a number of homofones. However, they rarely result in true ambiguity because they appear across parts of speech or case. While devoiced homophones do not cause misunderstanding, they are a frequent source of spelling erorrs for native speakers. They are also often used for word play.

Unvoiced stem Devoiced homophone
dup (stomp) dub (oak)
let (flight, of years) led (ice)
chlup (a hair [animal]) chlub (boast!)
řiť (anus) řiď (drive!)
les (forest) lez (crawl!)
zeť (son in law) zeď (wall)

Voicing assimilation

There are a few things that happen to individual sounds when put together. Especially consonants are vulnerable. If two consonants meet, the second always makes the first change its voicedness.1 For instance, in kde the voiced d changes the unvoiced k so that it is pronounced as voiced g. The pause is unvoiced so ending consonants are always pronounced unvoiced. Additionally, the following word always forces the change on the final consonant of the preceding word. Voiced consonants without an unvoiced pair (i.e. m, n, l, r, j) and v do not usually trigger assimilation.

Feminine genitive plural feminine and neuter

When the final vowel in a feminine or neuter model is preceded by two consonants, the first consonant is revoiced in Genitive Plural.

Sg Gen Pl
tužka tužek
kamarádka kamarádek
družka družek
hrobka hrobek
slůvko slůvek
lůžko lůžek

k > g voicing

When k is followed by a voiced consonant, it assimilates to the voiced g. Because non-assimilated g is almost always associated with loan words, Czechs do not realize that this is happening and will claim that they in fact pronounce k.

This voicing assimilation happens within as well as between words. It is most prominent in the very frequent wh- question words: kde, kdo, kdy which are pronounced gde, gdo, gdy.

The final k in jak (how) is often voiced as g when followed by a voiced consonant. For instance, jak do (how to) is pronounced jagdo.

ř devoicing

ř can also be devoiced. Voiceless ř is not an independent sound in Czech and most Czechs have no awareness of its existence. The voiced ř is unique to Czech but the voiceless ř can be found in Polish and other languages.

Devoiced ř appears in two contexts:

  1. In a consonant cluster where ř is the final consontant preceded by a voiceless consonant.

  2. When ř is the final consonant (usually in imperatives):

Most common patterns with devoiced ř:

Pattern Examples
kř křída, křest, křen, křesťan, skřítek
př před, přes, příklad, přítel, přát (si), spříst
tř tři, třída, třeba, třít, třást (se), střed, střelit, střep
-ř měř, miř, věř, zvěř

Consonant Clusters

Another prominent feature of Czech pronunciation is its tendency to cluster consonants. As many as 4 consonants can be in one syllable without any vowels. Thus, zmrzlina (icecream) is in fact a t-syllable word. Examples of monosyllabic words without any vowels are smrt, krk, vlk, smrk, pštros, strom, stvol.

6 consonants in a row can be found in verbs in the past tense such as scvrkl (shrank) forming two syllables and even a 8 consonant rarity could be contemplated in the verb scvrnkls (you flicked [sth] off a surface). There is also the famous Czech sentence Strč prst skrz krk which seemingly lacks vowels completely because r plays the role of the vowel.

Syllables

When you speak, it is not really the sounds you pronounce, it is syllables, words and sentences. Thus, when you practice pronunciation start putting the sounds into syllables and words. You will also find that then they are easier to pronounce.

All syllables have to have at least a vowel or a sound that plays the role of a vowel. In Czech, r and l can play the role of a vowel which is why it is possible to have Czech syllables with just consonants such as krk or vlk. It is possible to have have a syllable with just a vowel. In Czech, there are even two words a and i that are just a vowel. But it is not possible to have a syllable with just one consonant.

Each language has a typical syllable patterns, or combinations of vowels and consonants (VC). In Czech, these patterns are most typical.

CV 50% na, se, já, máma, Lída, kolo, jede, koruna
CVC 15% rok, sůl, nad, sám, Radka, krk, plk
CCV 10% sto, pro,
CCVC 8% proč, krok, strk, smrk, zmrzlina
CCCVC strom
CCCCVC pštros

Most words you find in text, will have three or four syllables. This is partly because most words have an ending added to them which often adds a syllable. Two syllable words are common but single syllable word are relatively rare. Mostly pronouns and prepositions.

Stress

Syllables are what carries stress. In Czech, it is always the first syllable that is stressed. Each sentence is divided into stress segments.

| Mám | rád | ovocné | knedlíky. |

| Dobrý | učitel | má | rád | své | studenty |

Notice, that the first syllable (in bold) is always stressed even when the vowel is short and the vowel in the following syllable is long. The unstressed vowels maintain their quality and are not reduced. This is very different from English. In English, only the stresed vowel is pronounced fully, the others are reduced.

Also, the stress segments are of different lengths. In English, the space between two stressed syllables is usually the same. English is a stress-timed language which means that vowels in unstressed syllables are reduced to keep the space between stresses roughly the same. For example, “give me a call” becomes “gimmeuh call” or “I’m going to” becomes “amana”. That’s how knock knock jokes work. Czech is syllable timed and the space between stressed syllables is more variable. This gives it a different rhythm.

These two features make it harder (but not impossible) to rap in Czech. But most importantly, they make it very challenging for English speakers to sound natural. This is the most important feature of Czech pronunciation to learn well.

Usually, one word occupies one stress segment but sometimes words combine in a way that the stress shifts between them. Usually, prepositions and some particles like mi, mu, si or se are combined with another word to be in a stress segment.

| Učili se | česky| od rána | do noci. |

| Měla jsem mu | ráno | zavolat. |

Intonation

Intonation Rules

There are basically two types of intonation in Czech:

  • simply descending which is used for simple statements and questions with question word

  • flat, rising on the last syllable which is used for YES/NO questions

    ! No matter what the intonation pattern, the stress is always on the first syllable of every word which gives the intonation a slight rising pattern on each word.

Statement intonation

**** Petr jede domů.
pe
tr
je
de
Mám se dobře.
mám
se
dob
ře

Wh- Question Intonation

Jak se máš?
jak
se
máš
Co děláš?
co
dě
láš
Co dělá Petr?
co
dě
lá
pe

YES/NO Question Intonation

Jede Petr domů?
je de pe tr do
Máš se dobře?
máš se dob

sections.title: Spelling
sections.content:
Spelling

Czech spelling is reputed to be very regular. It is true in that it is learnable. But it is not completely straightforward. The are basically three types of rules that are at work.

  1. Letter = sound: a certain combination is always pronounced in a certain way. For instance, if you see á you pronounce it as aaaargh.

  2. Letter combinations are pronounced in a certain way. For instance, ě in mě is pronounced differently than when it follows vě, or dě.

  3. Assimilation of consonants described in the chapter on Pronunciation

  4. Exceptions: Some words or patterns of words are known to be spelled differently from the rules 1-3. Most common with some uses of i vs y.

ABECEDA: Names of the letters in the Czech alphabet

á dlouhé á bé cé čé dé ďé é dlouhé é ef
gé há chá í dlouhé í jé ká el em en
ó dlouhé ó pé qvé er eř es eš té ťé

ú

s čárkou

ů

s kroužkem

vé dvojité vé iks ypsilon dlouhé ypsilon zet žet

!

  • ch is an independent character in Czech. It follows h in the alphabet and is so sorted in Czech dictionaries.

  • Notice that the accented character always follows the normal one in the alphabet.

  • Notice that the names of the short vowels are long vowels, and the long vowels are named as dlouhé (long).

Czech accent marks - Diacritics

´

čárka

used to lengthen vowels (the vowel is the same only twice as long)

can be used with all vowel with the same effect

ˇ

háček

used to soften consonants c, d, n, r, s, t, z

if d, t, n are followed by e the ˇ is placed over the e, when followed by i/í the ˇ is dropped (see below)

(Note: In print, háček ˇ over d and t is displayed as an apostrophe ’: ť, ď.)

°

kroužek

only used with u if it is not the first letter in the word; otherwise ´ is used. For instance, úkol vs domů or sůl

Spelling rules for i and ě

letter + letter is pronounced as in
n + i í ňi / ňí nyní
t + i í ťi / ťí titíž
d + i í ďi / ďí jdi
n + ě ňe něco
d + ě ťe tělo
t + ě ďe dělo
m + ě mně město
b/p/v + ě bje / pje / vje věc

The above chart describes how n, t, d, m, b, p, v are pronounced when followed by ě or i/í. Notice that the ě is pronounced as a regular e.

Use of y vs. i

The distinction between Y and. I is the most irregular phenomenon in the Czech spelling system. Both y and i denote identical sounds. Y is used regularly after all the hard consonants and never after soft consonants. Its use after ambiguous consonants is completely arbitrary and the words which use y have to be memorized by rote (even by native speakers.)

Basic rules of use of i and y after consonants

i
í

after ž, š, c, č, ř, j, ď, ť, ň

děti, život, žít, jít

after b, f, m , l , p, s, v, z in all words where y is not specifically required

bít, lid, dopis, vila

after l in past plural form of verbs if the subject is masculine animate

muži šli, Petr a Jana šli (masc. takes precendence)

y

ý

after h, ch, k, r, d, t, n

nohy, roky, ryba, rány

after b, f, m , l , p, s, v, z for prescribed words (can be found in Czech spelling manuals)

být, byt, mýt, lyže, sypat, vyjít, vykat, brzy, jazyk, …

after l in past plural form of verbs if the subject is not masculine animate

ženy a děti šly
! There are a few instances where i and y distinguish the meaning of two words. Most notably bít (to beat) vs být (to be) and mít (to have) vs mýt (to wash). In spoken language, however, these words are homonymous.

ú vs. ů

The only difference is the position in the word.

ú beginning of words úkol, úspěch, účet,
words where a prefix is added to the beginning of a word whose root begins with ú účet - zúčtovat, úhel - pravoúhlý
ů middle and end of word různý, způsob, Petrů

Using Capital Letters

Czech rules for the use of capital letters are different from English. Titles of books and articles, and names of states and institutions all capitalize only the first word. Only cities with two names capitalize both. Also not capitalized are names of days of the week and months. Even words like names of nations are not capitalized when used as adjectives. Names of languages are also not capitalized.

Punctuation

Czech punctuation rules are much stricter then those of English.

,

čárka

After all conjunctions except a, nebo, i.

Neví to, protože je hloupý. Není tu, ale poslal peníze.

Always to separate clauses.

Protože neměl peníze, nepřišel.

Always to separate inserts longer than one word.

Slíbil to, ale, protože neměl peníze, neudělal to.

;

středník

Rarely used in Czech texts, Czech typewriter keyboard doesn't even include it.

:

dvojtečka

Similar to English.

?

otazník

Similar to English.

!

vykřičník

Used always at the end of imperative sentences.

Not usually used for exclamations.

Jdi domů! (Go home!)

sections.title: Idioms, Phraseology and Vocabulary
sections.content:
Idioms, Phraseology and Vocabulary

This section describes the very important parts of language that usually fall somewhere between the grammar, dictionary and the phrasebook. You rarely find them in one place. But without them, you can never consider yourself to be proficient in a language.

The list here is not exhaustive and is presented from the point of view of an English speaking learner. We focused on things that are different from English and a common point of confusion. However, they are real patterns and learners coming from any language can benefit from them.

This section is forever incomplete. There is a long list of subsections in progress that may appear in future editions.

Words with a difference

This section is particularly English centric. It describes words the usage of which is in some special way different from English. Speakers of other languages may find them unremarkable. These differences go both ways, often speakers of Czech will make mistakes in English because of confusions arising from these words.

ask: zeptat se vs. požádat

There are two very distinct ways of asking. One is asking for information and the other is asking for a favor. This translates into two Czech words:

zeptat se

požádat

Zeptal se kolik je hodin.
(He asked what time it was.)

Požádal ho, aby odešel.

(He asked him to leave.)

Note: Often, říct [tell to] will be used instead of požádat. They asked him to leave. will be translated as Řekli mu aby odešel. [They told him to leave.]

How to say Czech in Czech

Where there is one word in English there are five in Czech.

čeština Czech language
Češka Czech woman
Čech Czech man
český, česká, české Czech (adj.) as in Czech Republic
česky Czech as in I speak Czech - an adverb

Compare this with the words for English!

angličtina English language
Angličanka English woman
Angličan English man
anglický, anglická, anglické English (tea)
anglicky English as in I speak English - an adverb
! Note that only the names of nationalities are spelled with a capital letter.

to cut in Czech

to (verb) (ipf, pf) a (noun)
cut (with scissors) stříhat, střihnout střih
cut (with an ax) sekat, seknout sek
cut (with a saw, knife) řezat, říznout řez

First in Czech

The word first has two equivalents in Czech in different contexts.

First from a group. Přišel první. He arrived first.
First in a sequence of activities. Nejdříve snídám. First, I have breakfast.

function/work

To describe something as functioning, Czech uses the metaphor of motion and not of work. Therefore, the word pracovat can never be used in this context. Here are some examples:

fungovat jít/chodit běžet
Motor funguje.
(The engine works.)		 Nejde mi počítač.
(My computer doesn’t work.)		 Naše televize už zase běží. (Out TV works again.)

Going on foot and by vehicle

Where English has one word meaning to go, Czech has two. One for going on foot, and second for going by a vehicle (car, bike, train, bus).

{width=“0.7903226159230097in” | {width=“1.0in” | height=“0.7903226159230097in”} | height=“1.0in”}
jít jet
jdu jdeme jedu jedeme
jdeš jdete jedeš jedete
jde jdou jede jedou
jít pěšky on foot
jet vlakem, autem, autobusem, na kole, na koni by train, car, bus; on a bike, horse

The same difference shows up in other verbs of motion as well. For example: nést (carry in hand) vs. vézt (carry by vehicle).

funny, happy, lucky vs. veselý, šťastný, směšný

There are many words in Czech to match the English funny, happy and lucky, but none of them are a perfect match.

funny (laughable) směšný happy (optimistic) šťastný
funny (amusing) zábavný happy (cheerful) veselý
funny (strange) podivný to be lucky mít štěstí

fun in Czech

There is no easy way to express the English word ‘fun’ in Czech, in all its contexts. Here are some example phrases. They often use words like zábava (entertainment), legrace (humour), prča (informal)

We’ll have fun. Bude zábava. Budeme se bavit.
They’re having fun. Dobře se baví.
She is fun. She is a fun person. Je s ní zábava. Je s ní legrace.

to know in Czech

vědět

+

že ..., co ..., kdo ..., kdy …, etc.

Vím, kdo jsi.

Víš, kde je Praha?

Víš, co to je?

I know who you are.

Do you know where Prague is?

Do you know what it is?

znát

+

Koho? Co?

Znám pana Pavla.

Znám Prahu.

Znáš Janu? Znám ji.

I know Mr. Pavel.

I know Prague.

Do you know Jana? I know her.

umět

+

infinitive

(noun, adverb)

Umím zpívat.

Umíš hrát košíkovou?

Umíš česky?

I can sing.

Can you play basketball?

Do you speak Czech?

!

Sometimes, the infinitive after umět is only assumed, and umět is followed directly by a noun or an adverb. E.g. Umím (vařit) polévku. or Umím (mluvit) česky.

Illnesses and treatments that are and that are not

Despite the advances in international medicine, there are still interesting differences in the popular terminology of different languages.

rýma cold Czech cure for a stuffy nose is to blow your nose. Even in public. Americans prefer to sniff. Mutually socially unacceptable.
angína tonsillitis Very common complaint for Czechs, often used for conditions not technically a tonsillitis but more of a soar throat.
angína pectoris angina Commonly confused in Czech-English translations.
nachlazení catch a chill Not as important a complaint in English (hence no noun). Czech cure is no ice-cream, keep warm and prevent drafts (průvan).
obklad compress Common Czech cure for soar throat, headache, sprains, etc.
pálení žáhy heartburn Seems slightly more common in English.
sádra plaster cast Seems to be a slightly more popular cure for broken and sprained limbs.
anestetikum novocaine Used only sparingly (for most serious operations) by Czech dentists. Brand as such not known to Czechs.

Jaký vs. Který / What vs. Which

This is a very easy distinction which is also infinitely tricky. The two Czech words correspond almost exactly to two English words. But in English what can often be used instead of which, which is very confusing when translated directly into Czech.

jaký

Jaký chceš rohlík?

Chci dobrý rohlík.

What roll do you want.

I want a good roll.

expresses quality independent of surroundings

který

Který rohlík chceš?

Chci ten nalevo.

Which roll do you want?

I want the one on the left.

chooses one out of a group of many

Jak vs. Jaký / Adverbs vs. Adjectives

This is an important distinction, which is also expressed in English, although not so strictly.

Jak se máš? Mám se dobře. Jaký je to banán? To je český banán.
How are you? I'm well. What kind of banana is it? It is a Czech banana.
Jak pracuješ? Pracuju pomalu. Jaká je tvoje práce. Moje práce je zajímavá.
How do you work. I work slowly. What is your work like? My work is interesting.

Ještě ne – Not yet vs. Už ne – Not anymore

Ještě ne – not yet Už ne – not anymore
Ještě to nevím. – I don’t know it yet. Už to nevím. – I don’t know it anymore.
Ještě jsem tam nebyl. – I haven’t been there yet. Už jsem tam nebyl. – I was not there anymore.
Ještě tam nebudu. – I won’t be there yet. Už tam nebudu. – I won’t be there anymore.

Use of je/jsou – is vs. there is

The Czech je has several uses that require slightly different translations into English. The translation may depend on word order or on the general meaning.

je = is, jsou = are

je = there is, jsou = there are

*Herec je ve filmu.* = The actor is in a film.

*Děti jsou doma.* = The children are at home.

*Ve filmu je herec.* = There is an actor in the film.

*Doma jsou děti.* = There are children at home.

Note: The same principle applies in the future (there will be/bude) and past (there was/byl).

Ještě – Still vs. Už – Already

Although relatively simple, these two words can cause quite a few problems. Compare their usage in negative and positive sentences. Notice how the meaning of už changes from past to present. With the future tense ještě and už can substitute for the future perfect in English, as in When you come, it will have been finished. – Až přijdete, už to bude hotové. Unlike their English equivalents, both ještě and už always appear in the beginning of the sentence.

Ještě – still Už – already, finally
Ještě jsem tady. – I’m still here. Už jsem tady. – I’m finally here.
Ještě jsem tam byl. – I was still there. Už jsem tam byl. – I was already there.
Ještě tam budu. – I will still be there. Už tam budu. – I will be there already.

Last in Czech - minulý vs poslední

Czech has two words to express the equivalent of the English last.

poslední

last in a series

Byl poslední. - He finished last.

latest event

poslední móda - latest fashion

minulý

past event

minulý rok - last year

minulý týden - last week

minulý čas - past tense

make vs. do vs. work

Most of the uses of the English make are translated by dělat/udělat into Czech. Only the sense of actually manufacturing something will use the verb vyrábět/vyrobit.

**dělat/udělat** (do, make, work)

pracovat
(work)

**vyrábět/vyrobit** (make)

Udělám dnes večer jídlo.
(I will make dinner tonight.)

Pracuju v kanceláři.

(I work in an office.)

Petr musel tu součástku vyrobit.

(Petr had to make that part.)

meet: potkat vs. setkat se

You can either meet someone by appointment or by accident. Czech has two separate words for this. Potkat means to meet by accident and setkat se means to meet by prior arrangement. Setkat se can also be expressed as mít schůzku (to have a meeting, appointment).

potkat setkat se
Petr potkal Janu na ulici.
(Petr met/bumped into Jana in the street.)		 Setkali se s prezidentem v deset hodin.
(They met the president at 10 o’clock.)

na vs. v

The prototypical meaning of na is on while the prototypical meaning of v is in. For a variety of places, though, na is used instead of v with the same meaning. For example, na Moravě.

countries that are islands or peninsulas Gibraltar, Hawaii, Island, Nový Zéland (but not Austrálie, Grónsko, Británie, Irsko, Itálie or Španělsko)
selected other countries Morava, Slovensko, Ukrajina, Podkarpatská Rus
local places on top of hills Vinohrady in Prague, or Kladno near Prague (people from outside the region may use v)
some institutions pošta, policie, univerzita, fakulta, gymnázium
selected places náměstí, diskotéka, výstava, nádraží
activities (as destinations) výlet, procházka, opera, hra, film

Translating no into Czech

The English word no has two different meanings which require two different words in Czech.

no as ne

no as žádný

Máte chleba? Ne, nemáme.

(Do you have bread? No, we don’t.)

Žádný student nenapsal test.

(No student wrote the test.)

Use of to (this vs. that)

The Czech to can be confusing because it can be translated as two different words:

to = this, that

to = it

To je problém. = This/that is a problem.

To je Karel. = This/that is Karel .

Bylo to dobré. = It was good.

Kdo je to? = Who is it?.

Sometimes, it is difficult to decide on a good translation.

there is/are in Czech

Czech doesn't have the construction there is/there are. Czech speakers have many difficulties mastering this construction in English.

You simply use 'je' or 'jsou'. Sometimes it is possible to use 'má' or 'mají' or even ‘existuje’.

there is a castle in Prague

v Praze je hrad

there are problems in the USA

v USA jsou problémy
v USA mají problémy
USA mají problémy

v USA existují problémy

Note that sometimes you must add 'tam' or 'tady', as in:

there's a car over there tam je auto
tam máme/mají auto
there's a car here tady je auto

Idioms, set expressions and useful patterns

Idioms are expressions that are usually used as whole chunks in which just a small part can be substituted. They also

Animal metaphors

lev lion hard working, strong
rys lynx great eyes
liška fox clever, crafty
sova owl wise
vlk wolf hungry
myš mouse quiet

Agreeing and disagreeing

I (don’t) agree. (Ne)Souhlasím Agreement Shoda/Dohoda

Mental and Physical Health/Feelings I am vs. it is vs. I have a

There are many phrases that cannot be translated directly from English to Czech. Often, groups of phrases have a similar translation. You need to memorize which phrases translate in what way. Most commonly, the literal translations oscillate between to have/to be or some other verb.

I am = mám/nemám

I’m thirsty. Mám žízeň. I’m hungry. Mám hlad.
I’m busy. Nemám čas. I’m free/available. Mám čas/volno.
I’m lucky. Mám štěstí. I’m not lucky. Mám smůlu.
I’m happy/glad. Mám radost. I’m depressed. Mám depresi.

I am = je mi

I’m cold. Je mi zima. I’m warm. Je mi teplo.
I'm sick. Je mi špatně. I’m well. Je mi dobře.
I’m sorry. Je mi líto.* I’m sad. Je mi smutno.

* I’m sorry only translates as je mi líto in the context of expressing regret and not in apologizing, where promiňte, or pardon is used. Another equivalent is mrzí mě.

I have (a) = mám

I have a cold Mám rýmu. I have a cough. Mám kašel.
I have flu. Mám chřipku. I have tonsillitis. Mám angínu.

I have a …ache = bolí mě …

I have a headache. Bolí mě hlava. I have a toothache. Bolí mě zuby.

it is = je + adverb (weather)

It is cold. Je zima. It’s nice. Je hezky.

I am = jsem

I’m glad.

Jsem rád.

I’m very happy.

Jsem šťastný.

Jsem veselý.

I am = a verb

I'm bored. Nudím se. I’m in a hurry. Spěchám.

Expressing Possibility and Necessity

Similarly to English, both of these can be expressed through modal verbs. For example,

Possibility/Impossibility Necessity/Lack of necessity
lze, nelze třeba, potřeba, zapotřebí
možno, možné nutno, nutné
asi nezbytné, nevyhnutné, neodvratitelné

Note: možná, třeba are also used as maybe.

Incorrect idioms resulting from confusion with English

Very often, what you say in English does not sound very Czech when translated literally. Here are a few examples of the more common mistranslations of English phrases.

No problem. Není problém. To je v pořádku.
Is it OK? Je to dobré? Nevadí to?
How are you? So-so. Jak se máte? Tak-tak. Jde to. Docela dobře.
I am happy. Jsem šťastný. Mám radost. Je mi dobře. Jsem veselý.
I have a question. Mám otázku. Můžu se zeptat?

Social interactions

Arranging appointments

We’ll meet at… Sejdeme se v/u… I will drop in later. Stavím se později.

Asking questions with negatives

Czechs often ask negative questions to show politeness where English would use would or just ask a direct question. For instance, Nevíte kde je tady nádraží?, Není tady pan Novák?, Nemáte housky? = Do you know where the train station is? Is Mr. Novák here? Do you have housky?

Nevíte, kde je nádraží? Where is the train station, please?
Nevíte, kolik je hodin? Would you know what time it is?
Nemáte rohlíky? Do you have rohlíky?
Nechceš jít dnes do kina? Would you like to go to movies?

Assurances

That’s OK. To je v pořádku. There's no hurry. To nespěchá.

Female forms of occupation names

učitel, řidič, fotograf, ředitel, -ka učitelka, řidička, fotografka, ředitelka
dělník, úředník -ice dělnice, úřednice
soudce, důchodce -kyně soudkyně, důchodkyně
vrátný -ý > -á vrátná
průvodčí, vrchní -í > -í průvodčí, vrchní

In Czech, most nouns for occupations have both a male and a female form. The female form is typically formed from the male form.

The vrátný/vrátná and vrchní models are conjugated as adjectives.

Two professions in particular are so commonly associated with females that they have no easy male equivalent. They are zdravotní sestra (nurse) and sekretářka (secretary). A male secretary could be asistent (although there is asistentka) or tajemník (which would be used for the Secretary of the UN). Sekretář would be used for a piece of furniture. There is no easy way of saying male nurse since sestra means sister.

Formation of Czech last names

All Czech women's surnames end in –ová and are conjugated as adjectives (with the exception of those ending in -ů).

pan paní manželé rodina
Novák +ová Nováková Novákovi+ Novákova++
Čapek +ová Čapková* Čapkovi Čapkova
Frýba +ová Frýbová Frýbovi Frýbova
Novotný** ý > á Novotná Novotní Novotných
Janků ů Janků Janků Janků***

* CeC + ová > CCová

** These surnames have the form of an adjective and they are conjugated using the hard adjective model.

*** Surnames ending in –ů are rare and are mostly derived from first names like Petrů, Karlů, Janů. They do not change their form. Equivalent surnames without the –ů also exist: Petr-Petrová-Petrovi.

+ These forms are conjugated according to the hard adjective plural model.

++ These forms are conjugated according to the possessive adjective model.

Liking in Czech (Mám rád ... a Líbí se mi ...)

Like things and people

In Czech, there are two ways of expressing your likes. You can either like the way something looks líbit se or like it for its properties mít rád. The difference is also grammatical. With mít rád the person who likes is the subject and the liked person or thing is the object (Petr má rád Martinu - Petr likes Martina). While with líbit se the liked person or thing is the subject and the person who likes is an indirect object (Komu? Čemu? [dative] case-see below). E.g. Líbí se mi Praha - I like Praha [Praha is pleasing to me-I like the way it looks].

mít rád
+ Koho? Co?		 líbit se komu
+ Kdo? Co?
mám rád Janu líbí se mi Jana I love (like) Jana vs. I like the way Jana looks
mám rád rohlíky líbí se mi rohlíky because they taste good vs. because they look funny
mám rád knihy líbí se mi knihy because they are interesting vs. because they look nice

mít rád is more general, and is never used with specific objects

mám rád ten rohlík líbí se mi ten rohlík I'm in love with this rohlík vs. I like the way it looks

Like food (chutnat)

If you want to say you like the food in front of you, you have to use chutnat; it has the same structure as líbit se

ten rohlík mi chutná ten rohlík se mi líbí I like this roll (tastes good) vs. I like it (it looks good)

Like to do

Here, you only use rád and the form of the verb.

Note: Rád has to reflect the gender and number of the subject: rád (man), ráda (woman), rádo (child), rádi (plural), rády (plural women or children)

rád + verb (NOT infinitive)
rád čtu I like to read
rád hraju tenis I like to play tennis
rád dělám úkoly I like to do homework

Negating rád

The word rád is negated differently if it is used about activities vs when it is used about people or objects. With mám rád, ne goes on the the verb mít. With rád + Verb, ne goes on rád.

mám rád knihy nemám rád knihy
rád čtu nerad čtu

Prosím in Czech – the multipurpose conversation glue

Zavři okno, prosím. Close the window, please.
Kávu, prosím. / Prosím jednu kávu Coffee, please. / One coffee please.
(Děkuju.) > Prosím. (Thank you.) > You're welcome.
Prosím. (Tady je ta kniha.) Here you are. (Here's the book.)
Prosím Tě. Please. (Informal)
Prosím Vás. Please. (Formal)

Prosím is either used as a particle or a verb. If used as a verb it is followed by a noun in the Koho? Co? case, e.g. Kávu prosím. It is the I form of the verb prosit (to ask, to beg, to plead).

prý, prej - I hear, they say

There is this little word prý (with its colloquial partner prej) which is used to report on things that you have heard from an unspecified source and may not be sure whether they’re true or not. It may be translated as I hear or They say into English. For example:

Prý bude letos drahý benzín. (I hear that gas will be expensive this year.)

How do you address people?

This is an issue of politeness. It is very important to know how to address people.

  • Rule 1: The ending of a name is changed when addressing the person (Michal - Michale).

  • Rule 2: In polite conversations, it is important to use the title if the person has one. Very much like in German. The name is not used after the title when addressing.

Going to see someone

Czech has two prepositions (similar to the French chez) that are usually translated into English as going to see someone or being at someone’s place.

u (being at someone’s)

k (going to see someone)

Dnes večer budeme u Katky.

(Tonight, we’ll be at Katka’s.)

Kde jsi? U zubaře.

(Where are you? At the dentists.)

Zítra půjdeme k babičce.

(Tomorrow, we’ll go to see granny.)

Musím jít k doktorovi.

(I must go see a doctor.)

Small talk

There is no expression in Czech to describe the English ‘small talk’. There is a word for ‘chitchat’ (pokec) or you can say ‘Přijďte si popovídat’ (Come over for a chat). But there is no word for ‘small talk’. Sentences like ‘they engaged in meaningless small talk’ or ‘she is no good at small talk’ are almost impossible translate into Czech.

Czechs have many fewer tools to engaged in small talk. There is no equivalent of the ‘how are you’ although that may be changing under the influence of American TV. Some phrases you can use on meeting people casually without necessarily wanting to know how they are:

  • Jak se vede? (How is it going)

  • (Tak) jak to jde? (How is it going)

  • Jak se daří? (How is it going?)

The response to these is something like:

  • Ale jde to. (Not bad)

  • No jo, to víte. Nestěžuju si. (You know. I don’t complaint.)

However, these phrases are not quite as formalized as they are in English.

Asking about other people is also common:

  • A co máma? (How about your mom?)

  • Jak se daří mámě?

  • Jak se vede bratrovi? (How is it going with your brother)

A common noncommital answer is:

  • Ale jo, jde to. (Not bad.)

  • No to víte, jak by to šlo. (You know, how could it be)

However, these are all rather informal and quite loose. A conversation can be built up from these blocks for a while.

Wishing good luck, trip, nice time, etc.

Have a nice weekend. Hezký víkend. Have a nice trip. Šťastnou cestu.
Have a good time. Dobře se bavte. Good luck. Hodně štěstí.
Enjoy yourself. Užijte si to. Fingers crossed. Držím ti palce.

What are the acronyms of academic titles used with people’s names?

Czechs use their academic titles with their names even outside strictly professional contexts. Czech uses a variety of acronyms that can precede or be appended to a person’s name. These are the most common titles ranked more or less by importance.

Mgr. magistr – MA RNDr. doktor – sciences specialization
Ing. inženýr – MSc CSc. kandidát věd –after name, not awarded any more
PhDr. doktor – PhD, general DrSc. doktor věd –after name, not awarded any more
JUDr. doktor – legal specialization Doc. docent – associate professor independent of a school
MUDr. doktor – medical doctor Prof. profesor - professor independent of a school

Text and conversation structure

a vs. i / and vs. as well

There is a significant differrence between i and a. 'i' means basically 'as well as' while 'a' means 'and'. Sometimes their meanings overlap slightly but there's always a subtle change in perspective.

a i
Byl tam Petr a Pavel Byl tam Petr i Pavel
Petr and Pavel were there. Petr and Pavel were both there.

When i occurs before a noun, it means even or as well: 'I Petr tam byl' - 'Even Petr showed up'/'Petr was there, as well'

You can even have a and i as part of the same clause in spoken language: 'A i Petr tam byl' - 'And Petr was there, too.'

Conditional with the infinitive

Sometimes in colloquial speech, the first part of a conditional sentence can be expressed through the infinitive.

Vědět to, nešel bych tam. If I had known it, I wouldn’t have gone there.

Být vámi, nedělal bych to. If I were you, I wouldn’t do it.

Telling stories about sequences of events

To tell a story, a lot of connecting words are needed:

teď Teď sedím doma a čtu si. Now I’m sitting at home and I’m reading.
předtím Předtím jsem se díval na televizi. Before that I was watching TV.
potom Potom si uvařím večeři. After that I will cook dinner.
později Později se půjdu na procházku. Later, I will go for a walk.
nakonec Nakonec půjdu spát. Finally (at the end), I will go to bed.

Strong and taboo language

Animal insults

prase pig dirty (not used for eating too much)
prasák pigman dirty (sexually suggestive) man
svině swine bastard, asshole (not very strong but extremely informal)
kráva cow bitch (stronger than cow in British English)
vůl ox moron (quite strong)
tele calf idiot, clueless, naive
kůň horse stupid (man) (not very strong and not very common)
slepice hen dismissive insult used to describe a woman
husa goose stupid (woman) – used often by women about women
koza goat stupid (woman) – used mostly by women (often self directed)
kozel billy goat randy old goat
ovce sheep easily led (same as English)
osel donkey stupid (man)

How do you swear in Czech?

The short answer is YOU don’t. In English, the acceptability of the most common swear words has increased greatly in the last few decades. While still considered inappropriate for children and mainstream broadcasting, they are more and more acceptable in many contexts. There are no such swearwords in Czech.

The most common Czech expletives have little to do with sex. While there are many sex-related taboo words, the common expletives have more to do with excreta. The following list gives the most common expletives and related euphemisms. Learners are strongly advised not to use them in any context.

Expletive

Euphemisms

English explanation

do prdele

do Prčic

do prkýnka

Expression of frustration. Literally: “to ass”

kurva

kurnik

kurňa

Stronger expression of frustration. Probably the closest to exclaiming Fuuck! in furstration. Literally: “whore”. When used as an insult, can be directed at men.

jdi do prdele

jdi do Prčic

jdi se bodnout

Expression of frustration directed at another person. Literally: “go to ass”

je to na hovno

stojí to za hovno

je to na houby

Dismissive expletive indicating low value of an object or idea. Literally: “shit”. Note: this is never used as an expresion of frustration.

já se na to vyseru

já se na to vykašlu

Expressing dissatisfaction with something or giving up on something. Roughly equivalent to fuck it, I give up but can also be used to describe someone not finishing something. Literally shit on something or in the euphemism cough on something.

posraný

podělaný

Adjective describing something negatively. Roughly equivalent to fucking or fucked up. Lit. shat on.

Dude! – ty vole

Even though vůl (ox) is an insult, in its Vocative form, vole, it can also be used to mean something equivalent to dude. You can often hear people sprinkle their speech (when addressing a very good friend) with ty vole. This is not an insult but is also completely inappropriate for any context outside extremely informal interactions with friends. For example, it would not be used within the family context.

Some people use vole or ty vole as a filler in their informal speech similarly to the way people overuse you know or you see in English.

Religious expletives and euphemisms

Expletives based on religion are no longer perceived as problematic. But there are still many old euphemisms that are used even if nobody perceives the full religious expletives to be blasphemous. They all have roughly the same meaning of expressing frustration and dismay.

Ježíši Kriste Jesus
Ježišmarjá Jesus Mary
pane Bože Lord
panenko Marie virgin Mary
hergot, herdek, hernajz from German Herr Gott
kruci, krucinál, kruci písek from Latin for cross
sakra, sakryš, sakra práce, sakramente from sacral
pro pána Jána, pro pána Krále for Lord John’s/King’s sake
mankote, šmankote from German mein Gott

Sex and genitalia taboo words and insults

Strong language related to sex or human genitalia is entirely inappropriate for learners. There are no neutral terms that would be acceptable in conversation and we strongly advise against attempting to use them even in jest if you look them up in a dictionary.

sections.title: Differences between standard and non-standard Czech
sections.content:
Differences between standard and non-standard Czech

As is usual in most languages, the Czech colloquial language has different pronunciation, and specific words and expressions. Unlike most languages, in Czech, the colloquial language also uses consistently different endings. For instance, you learn mladý (young) and hear mladej on the street, or you see Šumavský chléb (Šumava bread) written on a shelf in the bakery but people ask for Šumavskej chleba. As you see the difference is mostly in vowels.

It is also noteworthy that the Moravian 'dialect' uses many of the endings of the written standard, although not consistently, leading many Moravians to claim that they speak “better Czech” than Bohemians.

Which ‘Czech’ is taught to foreigners?

As a learner you don't have to worry too much about it, but it is important to keep in mind that you may hear some endings pronounced differently from how you learned them.

Choosing the right form can be a hard decision for a teacher to make. The standard variant is more regular but also more complex. If you started speaking colloquial Czech with beginners' mistakes it would sound ridiculous. The solution usually is, to use a simplified standard Czech and make it more communicative by introducing elements from the colloquial as appropriate.

The trick is that the two 'languages' are not always mutually exclusive. For two words in one sentence uttered by a Czech in normal everyday communication, you may find one ending colloquial and one literary, and there are no rules for this. Therefore, teachers cannot simply resolve to teach one or the other because except for in writing they are rarely separated. On top of that, Czechs themselves sometimes quarrel which is which.

The hard thing is to tell when to use which ending. The terms colloquial and literary or spoken and written are not very accurate. The colloquial variant is never used in writing (except, paradoxically enough, in literature), or for official purposes on TV, radio announcements, speeches, advertisements etc. You would use it with your friends but it is also used in less formal public situations like lectures, speeches to small audiences, etc.

Some differences between “standard” and “colloquial” Czech spisovná a nespisovná čeština

This is a very important feature of the Czech language. In reality, there are two language codes that are used for different occasions.

'Literary' and 'colloquial' are not the best terms to distinguish between the two varieties of present-day Czech, but they are the most commonly used ones. Better terms might be Standard Czech and Common Czech (used by H. Kučera in his The Phonology of Czech of 1961). Standard Czech is taught in schools, used in mass media, and most written documents, both official and unofficial. Common Czech is almost exclusively spoken. It is used in all personal communication, and also for semi-official purposes, including public speeches.

Although there are many differences in vocabulary, pronunciation, and syntax, the most pronounced disparity is in morphology. For some grammatical models there are two very different sets of endings. A short example is given below.

The main problem for a foreigner learning the two different codes is that the difference is often a matter of scale. Also, often in the spoken language standard Czech forms are mixed with common Czech ones.

Morphology Vocabulary
Trend Standard Common English Standard Common English
-ý/í > -ej mladý mladej young být bejt to be
-ý/í > -ej nosí nosej they wear chléb chleba bread
-é > -ý mladého mladýho of young mléko mlíko milk
-ý(í)m > -y(i)m vidím vidim I see méně míň less
o- > vo- okno vokno window mnoho moc many / much
-ami > -ama s ženami s ženama with women bysme bychom we would

The difference originated at the time of the National Revival, when the, then 200 years old, language of Bible Kralická was taken as the basis for standard Czech by the revivalists like Dobrovský. But in fact, even in the time of Blahoslav, many of these morphological forms had been out of common use. Czech was also developing parallel to this, mostly among the common people, and mostly out of the cities. This language was used for writing only by Catholic priests who were striving to be understood by their audience.

Examples of rules for converting from written to spoken Czech

Written Standard Spoken

Deleting

dcera cera
šestnáct šesnáct

Contracting or expanding

pojď sem pocem
nějak ňák
osm osum

Adding ‘v’ before ‘o’ at the beginning of words

oba voba
okno vokno
otevřít votevřít

Sometimes e is pronounced as í

haléř halíř
velké velký
velkému velkýmu

ý is pronounced as ej if it's a part of an adjective's ending

bílý bílej
dobrým dobrejm
těžkých těžkejch

-y/mi > -ma

studenty studentama
banány banánama
lidmi lidma
vámi váma
nimi nima
těmi těma

What you hear and what you read

What you hear people in the streets and shops say and what you read on signs around you can be quite different. Most textbooks teach you language on the more formal end of the scale (and for good reason because speaking highly colloquially with a thick accent and while making rudimentary errors would be ridiculous) but at the same time, they will tend to include words that do not sound out of place in the spoken language. Here are some very common examples of functiona words:

What you hear What you read What it means
už již already
všechno vše all
tady zde here
jenom jen, pouze only
hned ihned immediately
kromě mimo except for

Here are some examples of common nouns:

What you hear What you read What it means
mlíko mléko milk
chleba chléb bread
hospoda (restaurace) restaurace, restaurant restaurant
rajče rajské jablko tomato
jabko jablko apple
oblečení oděvy clothes
boty obuv shoes / footwear
jídlo potraviny food / groceries

Sometimes there is a similar difference in English e.g. the difference between boty/obuv is similar to that of shoes/footwear (i.e. footwear is more general) but you are still more likely to see obuv in shop windows than boty.

sections.title: Czech Trivia
sections.content:
Czech Trivia

What is the relationship of Czech to English or other languages?

Czech (along with English, German, French, Spanish, Greek, as well as Persian or Hindi, and dozens of other languages) belongs to the Indo-European family of languages. Languages from this family split out in about 4,000 BC, so by now they only have a few words in common (bratr - brother - frére, matka - mother - mére, and such). The only languages in Europe that don't belong to this family are Basque (which is on its own), and Hungarian, Estonian and Finnish (Finno-Ugric languages).

This large family has many branches, for instance, Germanic (English, German) or Romance (French, Spanish, Italian, Romanian). Czech belongs to the Slavic branch (together with Slovak, Polish, Russian, Bulgarian, Serbochrovatian, Bielorussian, Slovenian, and Ukrainian). Along with Polish and Slovak, Czech is a West-Slavic language.

This chart provides a summary of the relationship of Czech to other languages. Circles indicate genealogical closeness of a particular language to Czech. Typefaces differentiate between different types of languages. The typology here is very simplified.

The typology of languages as presented here is mostly based on morphology with some implications for syntax. Also, no language is strictly limited to one type, usually, the type indicates a general tendency. The four basic types are:

Inflecting Agglutinating Isolating Polysynthetic
Grammatical relationships expressed by: endings endings word order combinations of lexical items
Endings express: combination of many functions each ending a single function N/A N/A

What is the history of Czech?

The history of Czech, as it is known now, starts somewhere in the 15th and 16th century when the first Czech grammar and a new translation of the Bible were published. The beginnings of Czech spelling lie in the work of Master Jan Hus in the early 15th century. Of course, the history of Czech goes much further back in the past to the 9th century when the Slavic dialects that later gave birth to Czech were spoken in the area. The first written records come from the turn of the 13th and 14th centuries. The first translation of the Bible into Czech dates somewhere to the 1380s thus being the third in Europe after Italian and French. The use of Czech as a literary and official language receded slowly with the Thirty-Year War (in the 17th century). Czech was then replaced by German as the language used for official purposes in the Czech lands as the Hapsburgs took over. In the following centuries, Czech was mostly spoken by lower classes (especially in the country) although some Baroque literature was also written in Czech. However, compared to German and Latin, there are relatively few literary works in Czech from the Baroque period. That is why by the end of the 18th century Czech was believed to be a dying language by many scholars of Czech origin.

The turn of the century, however, witnessed the birth of a cultural and political movement referred to as the National Revival or Awakening (Národní Obrození). A new Czech grammar book and a large dictionary were published. Speaking Czech became fashionable, and many works of literature were published in the language including some high profile faked historical texts. As the century progressed, Czech found its place along with German as the official language, and was beginning to be taught in schools of higher education again. Since 1918 (founding of Czechoslovakia), Czech has been the sole official language in the Czech Republic. You can see some of the most important dates of the development of the language in the chart below.

Some important dates in the history of Czech language

863 Christian Mission of Cyril and Methodius to Great Moravia - liturgy in Old Church Slavonic - New Testament translated. Local Slavic tribes spoke a variety of dialects which were similar to Old Church Slavonic.
1000s Beginnings of Czech State. No written Czech documents. Beginnings of western influence.
1100s Latin replaced Old Church Slavonic as liturgical, administrative, and literary language.
1200s First written Czech materials, at first, mostly annotations of Latin works which, towards the end of the century, developed into more extensive works such as legends and chronicles.
1313 Dalimilova Kronika - the first big chronicle written in Czech, based, to a large extent on earlier Latin works of similar content.
1348 Founding of Prague University (today's Charles University) began a period of Czech translations of official and other documents culminating with a Czech translation of the Bible from Latin Vulgata. First Latin/Czech dictionaries/word lists were also compiled at that time.
1412 Master Jan Hus' De Ortographia Bohemica - an influential work codifying Czech writing system which became the basis of the writing system used today.
1499 Viktorín Kornel ze Všehrd wrote first work of scientific rigor in Czech concerned with the contemporary legal system. This work inspired translations of classical works from Greek and Latin.
1533 First Czech grammar by Beneš Optát, Petr Gzel and Václav Filomates.
1571 Czech Grammar by Jan Blahoslav started work which ultimately led to a new translation of the Bible.
1593 Bible Kralická - new translation of the Bible directly from the Greek and Hebrew original. Later during the national revival, it became one of the sources for codification of Czech literary language.
1627 After the lost battle of White Mountain (1620) German was pronounced equal to Czech as the official language of Czech state administration and courts, which, in effect, caused the actual disappearance of Czech from official documents by the end of the century. This was due, mostly, to lack of Czech officials and scribes at the courts of prevailing foreign nobility. Ultimately, this led to the ousting of Czech as the official language from schools and state administration offices.
1600s
-1700s		 Baroque period in the Czech lands - formative period for today's Czech colloquial language. Although this period is usually connected with the degeneration of the Czech language, it witnessed the creation of such works as Czech grammars written in Latin (1672), and the Czech printing manual (1668), and Defenses of the Czech Language which were the overture to the Czech national revival.
1790s -1860s Czech National Revival - a cultural and political movement which set out to revive Czech language and culture. Among the names that are usually associated with the movement at its different stages are: J. K. Tyl, J. Dobrovský, Lad. Čelakovský, J. Jungman, Fr. Palacký, and many others. This period saw founding of the first Czech newspaper, translations of famous literary works as well as active development of original Czech literature, and introduction of Czech to schools (1850).
1809 Dobrovský's Czech grammar Ausführliches Lehrgebäude der böhmischen Sprache.
1835 First volume of Czech dictionary (with German equivalents) by Josef Jungman was published (the last volume came out in 1839). A major lexicographical work, unsurpassed for over a century, which had a great formative influence on the Czech language. Jungman used vocabulary of the Kralická Bible period and of the language used by his contemporaries. He borrowed words not present in Czech from other Slavic languages (e.g., Polish, Russian, Serbian). He also inspired development of Czech scientific terminology, thus, making it possible for original Czech research to develop.
1836 Publication of Máj by Karel Hynek Mácha. This poem not only marked the beginning of Romanticism in Czech literature, but was also the first original poetic work of such magnitude in the Czech language. To this date, it is considered one of the gems of Czech literature.
1918 Founding of Czechoslovakia with Czech and Slovak as the official languages. Especially, the 1930s were a time of very intensive literary and publishing efforts.
1948 Beginning of state intervention into language politics. Only one, state-approved, curriculum, was taught at schools. Although Russian was compulsory at all levels of the education system, there is very little Russian influence on Czech from this period.
1989 Decentralization of language education. Beginning of English influence on Czech with the influx of new technology and business practices. Later in the 1990s, new reference works are published. In 1994, the project of Czech National Corpus is launched (http://ucnk.ff.cuni.cz).

What type of language is Czech?

Inflecting, would be a linguist's answer. This linguistic term means that Czech words have different forms depending on their function. The one consequence of this for learning Czech is that if you learn a new word, you are not necessarily able to use it 'correctly' (i.e. in its right form) in all possible contexts. You also have to learn what its other forms are in order to you use it so that it says what you want it to say.

Conversely, working with the dictionary you may not be able to look up words as you see or hear them. You have to know how they changed to their present form. So, for instance, oči (eyes) you won't find in the dictionary under oč (as you would English eyes) but as oko which is the basic dictionary form.

In English (an analytic language but none the easier), words are either put in the right order (John loves Mary vs. Mary loves John kind of thing), or helping words such as have, do, of, etc. are used. Hence, instead of different forms and endings, you have to learn all the subtleties of word order to be able to use new words so that they mean what you want them to mean. It is generally easy to look up words in the dictionary as even irregular verbs (go-went-gone) are listed.

As an example of how different forms of a word change the meaning of a sentence, let us compare a few sentences in Czech and in English. For instance, in the two following English sentences

A. A patient teacher teaches a clever pupil.

B. A clever pupil teaches a patient teacher.

to get the pupil to teach the teacher, all you have to do is swap their positions in the sentence. The words remain the same, their form doesn't change.

In Czech, it does not matter who goes first. What is important, though, is the form of the two parties. So in Czech A. and B. would mean the same thing if you didn't change the form of the words, as below.

A1. Trpělivý učitel učí chytrého žáka. A patient teacher teaches a clever pupil.
A2. Chytrého žáka učí trpělivý učitel. A patient teacher teaches a clever pupil.

They are not the same if you do change their forms, and don't change the word order.

A1. Trpělivý učitel učí chytrého žáka. A patient teacher teaches a clever pupil.
B. Trpělivého učitele učí chytrý žák A clever pupil teaches a patient teacher.

In principle, it is pretty easy to learn how to go back and forth between different forms and their meanings, although, just as for a learner of English it takes time to learn to always use the right word order, it will take time for you to learn to always use the right form, but by then you will be able to communicate freely, and have time to focus on correctness.

Which words have different forms and when?

Most words in Czech do most of the time. All nouns, adjectives, pronouns, and numerals change their forms according to case, gender, and number. Verbs change their forms according to person and tense (like in English). So, for instance, in mluvím (I speak) -ím has the same role as I.

The words that don't change their forms are adverbs, prepositions, and conjunctions.

Are there polite forms of verbs like in French or German?

Yes, there are. They are used similarly to French. We also use the second person plural2 when speaking with someone we respect or don't know very well. Qu'est que tu as? vs Qu'est que Vous avais? (in French) = Co máš? vs Co máte? (in Czech).

You can always tell the informal form by the ending -š and the formal by -te. The pronouns used for pointing at people are Ty (you – informal) and Vy (you – formal).

What do the days of the week mean?

Unlike in English, where the names of the days of the week are mostly derived from the names of Norse gods, the Czech names have mostly easily identifiable meaning which can be useful a useful mnemonic device for the student.

Note that the Czech week begins with Monday. It is important to keep in mind when comparing calendars.

Note that just like names of the months, names of the day always begin with a small letter.

pondělí The day after Sunday (do nothing day), i.e. po neděli.
úterý The only obscure one: from the old Slavic vtoroj (second). Compare with Russian for Tuesday vtornik.
středa The middle day, from střed (middle).
čtvrtek The fourth day, from čtvrtý (the fourth)
pátek The fifth day, from pátý (the fifth)
sobota Quite obviously derived from the word Sabbath.
neděle Do-nothing day, from nedělat (do nothing)

What do the names of months mean?

Now, they mean very little and, for some of them, most Czechs would not know the origin, or would mistake it for something else. Others, however, are very clear.

leden Month of led (ice). Derives clearly from the Czech word led (ice) since it describes a period when everything is covered with ice. January
únor Month of ice breaking and sinking in the water. It comes from a word nořit (to submerge, sink). For most Czechs, this is rather opaque. February
březen Month of birch trees (bříza) March
duben Month of budding oaks (dub) April
květen Month of flowers (květy) May
červen Month of worms (červy). Worms were used for making red (červený) dye. June
červenec The same etymology. July
srpen Month of harvest with sickle (srp) August
září Month of rutting (za říje = at the time of rutting) September
říjen Month of rutting (říje = rut) October
listopad Month of falling leaves (list = leaf, padat = to fall) November
prosinec Month of gray color (from Old Czech – has no present-day equivalent) December

Seasons and names of the months

Co? (what) Kdy? (when)
zima leden v zimě v lednu
(winter) únor v únoru
březen v březnu
jaro duben na jaře v dubnu
(spring) květen v květnu
červen v červnu
léto červenec v létě v červenci
(summer) srpen v srpnu
září v září
podzim říjen na podzim v říjnu
(autumn) listopad v listopadu
prosinec v prosinci

Note that the names of the months never begin with a capital letter.

Spelling out

Because Czech spelling works by and large on the what you see is what you say principle, Czechs almost always know how a name or a word is spelled. Therefore, if you want to spell out your name to someone, pronounce it as if it were written in Czech. For example, Joan would be yo-ah-n and John something like yo-eh-n both pronounced as single words with three syllables.

Because they have no training in it (and no need for it), Czechs often have trouble visualizing a word quickly based simply on hearing a sequence of letters. That’s why using the English approach of spelling by naming all the letters, even using the Czech names, can cause problems. Of course, sometimes it is necessary to specify the letter by name but then only that one letter is singled out after the whole word was pronounced.

How many endings does Czech have?

Theoretically, for nouns there could be 196 different endings (14 different functions - 6 + 1 cases in the singular and 6 +1 in the plural - times 14 different models). In fact, there are only 24 different endings: -a, -e/ě, -i, -o, -u, -y; -ou; -é, -í, -ů; -ech, -ách, -ích; -em, -ám, -ím, -ům; -mi; -ami, -emi, -ími; -ovi, -ové, and 0 - nothing is also considered an ending. But you will see that they have much in common, for instance, m, ch, v are always used for similar functions.

There are some more endings for adjectives but no more than ten. Overall, there are fewer than 40 endings for all nouns, adjectives, pronouns and numerals which is not much at all.

There are 4 basic verbal models which gives us 32 options (with sub-models 78) with about 18 ending forms that are actually distinct from one another.

Then, there are about a dozen endings used for other purposes, and that's about it. Apparently, Czech, the language of endings, makes do with about 60 different endings altogether. If we consider that there are several hundred irregular words (both verbs and nouns) in English, this is not bad at all. This is not to say that endings is all that there is to learning Czech, just as irregular verbs are not all that there is to learning English.

Are there many dialects of Czech?

The question of what is a dialect and what is an accent is a very complicated one. As for many modern languages, differences between dialects are growing less and less pronounced. For Czech, historically prominent dialects are confined to small regions, and are slowly dying out, mostly because of the influence of the media. Traces of historical dialects can be found in the standard language of different regions, but very few people speak something that could be identified as a pure dialect.

In the popular perception, there are two widely recognized dialects: Moravian (which is in fact three quite distinct dialects with quite a few different words and expressions), and Bohemian. Most people can identify the difference primarily by accent and some prominent vocabulary differences.

Among accents that are readily recognized is the fairly strong Prague accent and the northern Morvian accent with influences from Polish. The Czech Roma minority also speaks Czech with a recognizable accent.

The difference between the written standard and colloquial language is often more pronounced than that between different dialects. Some of the Moravian dialects also use some ending that are notably identical to the written standard Czech.

Is there anything about Czech that is easy?

Yes, a number of things. The tenses, for instance. There is no sequence of tenses (a common threat to a learner of English of which you even may not be aware). Also, Czech does not have articles. It is very easy to learn Czech spelling, too. In some respects Czech is more regular than English. It has very few irregular verbs. On the other hand it does abound with exceptions in nouns. The stress is always on the first syllable but there are short and long vowels that are independent on it.

All in all, it is almost impossible to say what is easy and what is hard. There are certainly many things in any language which are cursed by its learners but still, countless brave men and women are undertaking the dangerous venture, lured by the promise of acquiring the key which will fling the gates to another culture wide open. Such a prize always makes this adventurous enterprise well worth all the effort.

Common Learner Errors

The most visible errors are those of morphology. Czech cases and conjugation of verbs are often the source of mistakes made even by more advanced learners. Inflectional rules, however, are easy to memorize because for the purpose of learning the language they are largely arbitrary. (Only, palatalization of roots with some endings makes this a little more difficult.) Also, native speakers take these errors for what they are, and don't consider them disruptive to communication.

On the other hand, learners of non-Slavic languages have grave problems with the Czech verbal aspect. Aspect, like articles and tenses in English, is hard to describe in terms of 'if-then' rules. To learn it properly, one needs to acquire a 'Czech perspective' on time and activity. Moreover, erroneous use of aspect is often detrimental to communication, as native speakers don't recognize them as errors but rather substitute other meanings.

Pronunciation is also important to successful communication. Good pronunciation is regarded as an indicator of good knowledge of the language by the native speakers. Well pronounced, even errors of aspect don't seem so bad.

Several aspects of pronunciation commonly pose difficulties for learners of Czech as a foreign language. Long vowels distinguish meaning in Czech (for instance, být vs. byt – to be vs. apartment). The length of the long vowel is approximately double of the short vowel. Stress in Czech is always on the first syllable. Only some prepositions take on the stress. Long vowels are pronounced long even in unstressed position (e.g. léta vs. létá – summers vs. he flies).

Another difficult feature are consonant clusters. R and l can function as sonant units in Czech syllable. An example can be a popular Czech tongue twister with no vowels Strč prst skrz krk (Put your finger down your throat). Of unique and difficult sounds, Czech boasts ř, basically trilled r which is not in any other language (except for Polish and some dialects of French).

Another class of errors altogether are those of idioms and vocabulary. Most of the Top 10 Mistakes are of this origin. Short of listing the most common ones, however, it is impossible to provide an informative classification.

Czech syntax is traditionally described as free. It is seen as some compensation for the complex morphology. This apart from being far from the truth, leads to neglecting syntax in Czech textbooks. Among other things, word order in Czech is used to differentiate between given and new information. For instance, Petr viděl Janu and Janu viděl Petr, superficially both meaning Petr saw Jana, both imply a different context. They might be paraphrased as It was Petr who saw Jana and It was Jana whom Petr saw. Which, of course, in English would be considered two very different sentences.

Part of Czech's reputation as a difficult language also comes from the fact that Czech native speakers don't have as much experience in dealing with people who are learning the language. While we always appreciate the effort, we may not always be ready to overlook errors and focus on communication. This also had to do with how foreign languages are taught in Czech schools where correctness is often put above communication.

In his book Chrám i tvrz (A Cathedral and a Fortress), Pavel Eisner a famous Czech writer, translator and an excellent philologist wrote that Czechs are differently sensitive to different kinds of errors. In speaking about the sensitive and vulnerable points of Czech he wrote:

“For us, mistakes in cases and collocations are very conspicuous but we accept them easily, often laughing, when we realize that the speaker is a foreigner. Mistakes in the complex laws of aspect, however, we feel are very awkward although we can admit that it is extremely hard for a non-Czech to master this devilish grammatical complexity of the Czech language. We react most vividly, also, at any deviation from the vowel length and the correct placement of stress.”

sections.title: Czech Grammar as Czechs Learn It
sections.content:
Czech Grammar as Czechs Learn It

This section lists the key terms used to talk about Czech grammar by Czechs. All Czech children will have been taught these terms (although some will remember them less well than others). Knowing these terms will be useful to you when you communicate with your teachers or read Czech textbooks. The Czech terms don’t always match English grammatical terminology perfectly but where equivalents exist, it should be fairly easy to understand how they relate to one another. This section is based on the work of teachers working for US Peace Corps Pre-Service Training in Summer 1996.

Word classes (parts of speech) - slovní druhy

There are 10 word classes recognized in the grammar of the Czech language:

Nouns podstatná jména
Adjectives přídavná jména
Pronouns zájmena
Numerals číslovky
Verbs slovesa
Adverbs příslovce
Prepositions předložky
Conjunctions spojky
Particles částice
Interjections citoslovce

The first 5 classes change their form in different contexts. The changes in 1 – 4 are called declension. The changes in verbs (5) are called conjugation.

Classes 6 – 10 do not change their form (with one minor exception).

Nouns – podstatná jména

When we talk about nouns, we indicate their: CASE 1st - 7th (pád)
NUMBER singular or plural (číslo)
GENDER masculine, feminine or neuter (rod)
MODEL pán, muž, čaj, žena, kuře, ... (vzor)
These are the names of cases: nominative 1. pád 1st case Kdo? Co?
genitive 2. pád 2nd case Koho? Čeho?
dative 3. pád 3rd case Komu? Čemu?
accusative 4. pád 4th case Koho? Co?
vocative 5. pád 5th case Kdo!Co!
locative 6. pád 6th case Kom? Čem?
instrumental 7. pád 7th case Kým? Čím?

Note: In Czech school grammar, cases are not given names but simply numbers and are always presented with the appropriate What/Who question for clarity. Academic grammars use the internationally recognized Latinate names.

Adjectives – přídavná jména

When talking about adjectives, we can identify these features: CASE as nouns (pád)
NUMBER as nouns (číslo)
GENDER as nouns (rod)
KIND hard, soft and possessive (druh)

Pronouns – zájmena

For pronouns, we can identify these features: CASE as above
NUMBER as above
KIND personal, possessive, demonstrative, reflexive, relative, interrogative, indefinite and negative
Examples of different kinds of pronounce: PERSONAL já, ty, on, ona, (ono), my, vy, oni
POSSESSIVE můj, tvůj, jeho, její, ...
DEMONSTRATIVE ten, ta, to, tento, tato, tamta, ...
REFLEXIVE se, si, sám, ...
RELATIVE který, jaký, čí, kdo, co (they start a clause)
INTERROGATIVE který, jaký, čí, kdo, co (they start a question)
INDEFINITE někdo, nějaký, něco, málokdo, ...
NEGATIVE nikdo, nic, nijaký, žádný, ničí, ...

Numerals - číslovky

When we talk about numerals, we can identify: CASE as above
KIND cardinal, ordinal, multiplication and generic
Examples of numerals of different kinds: CARDINAL jedna, dva, tři, čtyři, ... (one, two, …)
ORDINAL první, druhy, třetí, ... (first, second, …)
MULTIPLICATION jednou, dvakrát, třikrát, ... (once, twice, …)
GENERIC jedny, dvoje, troje, ... (a pair of, two pairs of, ...)

Verbs - slovesa

For verbs we can identify these features: PERSON 1st, 2nd or 3rd (osoba)
NUMBER as above (číslo)
TENSE past, present or future (čas)
VOICE active or passive (rod)
MOOD indicative, imperative, conditional (způsob)
ASPECT perfective or imperfective (vid)
CATEGORY 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th (5th) (druh)

Here are some examples to give you an idea of what to imagine under verb categories:

*dělám:* I'm doing 1st person, singular, present, active, imperfective, 2nd category, and indicative mood in the following sentence: Dělám domácí úkol.
*nespi (!):* don't sleep 2nd person, singular, present, active, imperative, imperfective, 4th category
**byl postaven:** was built 3rd person, singular, past, passive, perfective, 3rd category, and indicative mood in the following sentence: Tento hrad byl postaven v 11. století. (This castle was built in the 11th century.)

Adverbs - příslovce

Adverbs express various circumstances of events (place = místo, time = čas, reason = důvod, manner = způsob) or grade of quality. They join verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.

Here are some examples of types of adverbs:

tady (here - place) brzy (early/soon - time) proto (therefore - reason)

rychle (quickly - manner) velmi (very - grade of quality)

Prepositions - předložky

There are many prepositions in the Czech language. After certain prepositions we use certain cases of nouns. Sometimes the case you use changes the meaning of the preposition.

These prepositions take only one case:

od, do, z(ze), u, blízko, vedle, kromě, bez Koho?Čeho?
naproti, k(ke), proti Komu?Čemu?
pro, přes, skrz, mimo Koho?Co?
po, o, v (ve) Kom?Čem?
s (se) Kým?Čím?

These prepositions take two different cases to express different meanings:

Kde? Kam?
Na Kom?Čem? Koho?Co?
nad, mezi, pod, před, za Kým?Čím? Koho?Co?

Czech prepositions, unlike English, are always followed by other words - they never occur at the end of a sentence.

Dům, o kterém jsem mluvil, ... The house I talked about ...
Na koho čekáš? Who are you waiting for?
Je těžké s ním pracovat. He is difficult to work with.

Moreover, unlike English, there are no “prepositional adverbs” in Czech.

Od té doby jsem tam nebyl. I haven't been there since.
Nikdo v domě není. There is nobody in.

Conjunctions - spojky

They connect clauses, or words in sentences. Here are some common conjunctions:

a, i, nebo, ale, když, protože, že, kdyby

Note that Czech prepositions (with the notable exception of a) are always preceded by a comma.

In Czech, you always have to use the conjunction že for that in the following sentences:

Myslím si, že to vím. I think (that) I know it.
Vím, že mám pravdu. I know (that) I am right.

Particles - částice

They usually start a sentence and they indicate the kind of the sentence question, command, exclamation. They often express wishes.

Ať žije královna! Long live the Queen!
Kéž by pršelo! I wish it rained!

Interjections - citoslovce

They express moods, emotions and will. They point to someone or something, or mark voices or noise.

ach (oh), au (ouch), br (sound make to indicate a feeling of cold), fuj (yuck), bác (bam), bim – bam (sound indicating bell tolling), haf (woof), ...

Word order - Slovosled (Syntax)

The Czech sentence (or clause) is described as having two basic parts:

subject predicate (verb)
podmět Přísudek
Petr čte.
Petr reads.

This core can be extended by an object (předmět):

subject predicate (verb) object
podmět Přísudek předmět
Petr Čte knihu.
Petr Reads a book.

Each of these core parts of the sentence (větné členy) can be further elaborated by adding adjectives and/or possessive pronouns to the nouns, and adverbs and/or prepositional phrases to the verbs.

The order of words in a sentence is used to emphasize certain words. The words that are placed towards the end of the sentence are emphasized.

Acknowledgements and licensing details

Origins of the Navigator

The Czech Language Navigator as a whole is an original creation based on materials developed for the US Peace Corps language program in the mid 1990s (referred to in previous editions as the Yellow Pages of the Czech Language). The Navigator adds to the cumulative grammatical knowledge of many generations.

It is impossible to compile an entire grammar book completely from scratch. The information in this Navigator is based on the reframing of information from reference materials too numerous to list. Some portions of this text contain original analysis (most significantly aspect) and all explanations are original. But the main contribution is in the compilation. Many people contributed to the original drafts over a period of several years.

Some of the sections were composed as separate handouts over many years of teaching and therefore, there is a certain inconsistency of presentation and tone of language. It is possible that this also resulted in some small portions of the text being copied from elsewhere without attribution as is common in the practice of busy teachers putting together handouts. We tried to replace all of these with original work but some may have been overlooked. We will be happy to remove these when pointed out or provide attribution.

Licensing and reuse

This work is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International. Under Commercial use we understand print for profit but not print distribution that charges for the cost of print and delivery. Neither do we consider commercial use using this work as a textbook in commercial courses, provided students are not charged for the text beyond the cost of reproduction.

We welcome and encourage the following reuse:

  • Corrections of errors and misprints (because of the frequent switching between Czech and English

  • Alternative formatting of charts and tables

  • Replacing or adding examples

  • Clarifying exisitng or adding alternative explanations

  • Adding new sections

  • Translation of the English into other languages

  • Transforming the content into other formats, including interactive apps

We have learned over many years that there is no one way to present grammar that will suit all learners and teachers alike. This reference is intended to be as complete a starting point as possible but does not claim to be the ultimate book.
